# Scaling Laws for Dense Retrieval: a scaled-down illustration, with an audit

*Companion report for the SIGIR '24 paper "Scaling Laws For Dense Retrieval" (Fang, Zhan, Ai, Mao, Su, Chen, Liu; arXiv 2403.18684v2). All numbers in this report are generated by script from `data/results/*.json`, `data/results.csv` and `data/results_summary.csv`.*

* **UNVERIFIED:** A4 (Group of 2–3 students); C18 (Mixed precision); D6 (Train loss vs eval loss comparable (to discuss over-fitting)?).

**Use this wording:** "in a heavily scaled-down setting, loss moves in the same direction as in the paper". **Do not write** that the paper was reproduced.

## 1. Executive summary

**Paper says** (Sec. 1, Sec. 4.1–4.2, Fig. 3–4): the test loss of dense retrieval models, measured by a continuous "contrastive entropy", follows a power law in model size and in the number of annotated pairs.

**Our experiment shows** (Sec. 6 below): with 5 BERT sizes (N from 512,128 to 86,235,648 non-embedding parameters), D = 10,000 training pairs and 3 seeds, the mean loss falls from 0.7265 to 0.1581 nats. With BERT-Small and D from 2,500 to 40,000 pairs it falls from 0.3658 to 0.1596. A 2-parameter power law fits both sweeps well (R² on the log scale 0.986 and 0.989; exponents 0.299 and 0.285) and the exponents are stable when one point is left out (0.259–0.320 and 0.267–0.294).

**Caveats that matter:** (1) our runs last 60–939 optimizer steps, the paper fixes 10,000 (Sec. 3.4); (2) the 3-parameter exponent of the data sweep is unstable (0.260–0.770 under leave-one-out); (3) two adjacent pairs (Small vs Medium, D = 10,000 vs 20,000) are not separated by the seed-to-seed spread; (4) the metric is a negative log-likelihood in nats, **not** a perplexity: the "Contrastive Perplexity" [OLD-LABEL] axis label in the original plots was wrong and is corrected here; random scoring would give ln(257) = 5.549.

## 2. Background for newcomers

**Information retrieval (IR)** is finding the documents (here: short text passages) that answer a query. **Dense retrieval** does this with neural networks: an *encoder* turns every query and every passage into a list of numbers (a vector, also called *embedding*). A passage is judged relevant when its vector points in nearly the same direction as the query vector; the score is the dot product. Because passage vectors can be computed once in advance, search over millions of passages is fast.

*Example.* Query "capital of California" and passage "Sacramento is the capital of California" should get a high score; a passage about football should get a low one (Figure F2).

**Training with a contrastive loss.** The model sees a query with one labelled relevant passage (the *positive*) and many random wrong passages (*negatives*). The scores of all candidates are turned into probabilities with a softmax. The loss is the negative logarithm of the probability given to the positive: it is 0 if the model puts all probability on the positive and large if it does not. This is the *negative log-likelihood (NLL)*, measured in *nats* (natural logarithm). With K candidates, a model that guesses at random gets ln(K); here K = 1 + 256 = 257, so ln(K) = 5.549 (Figure F3, F10).

**Scaling law.** In many neural networks the loss falls as a smooth power law, L ≈ a·X^(−α), when the model size N or the data size D grows. On log–log axes this is a straight line whose slope is −α. If it holds, small, cheap experiments can predict large ones, which is why the topic matters; the paper argues it also helps allocate a budget between annotation and compute (Sec. 5).

## 3. What the paper says

*(Every statement cites the section, figure, table or equation of arXiv 2403.18684v2. Metadata verified against Crossref and the arXiv API: SIGIR '24, Washington DC, July 14–18 2024, pp. 1339–1349, DOI 10.1145/3626772.3657743.)*

**Paper says:** the research questions are how model size, annotated-data size and annotation quality affect dense retrieval (Sec. 1, Sec. 4 opening).

**Paper says:** the encoder is a pre-trained Transformer with a projection layer, shared by queries and passages, scored by inner product (Sec. 3.1–3.2, Eq. 1–2, 4); training uses random and in-batch negatives, 256 negatives per step, a fixed 10,000 steps (Sec. 3.4, Eq. 3). Learning rate, batch size and temperature are not stated in the text (UNVERIFIED in the paper).

**Paper says:** the evaluation metric is the "contrastive entropy", the NLL of Eq. 5 with 256 random negatives per test pair; a 100,000-passage sub-corpus is used in the metric study; it correlates with MAP@10, NDCG@10 and Recall@1000 (Sec. 3.5, Fig. 2), with a possible "emergent" jump near 0.25.

**Paper says:** N is the number of non-embedding parameters, from 0.5M (BERT-Tiny) to 82M (BERT-Base) (Sec. 3.2 and its footnote 2; Fig. 6 legend); the Introduction says "0.5 to 87 million" (Sec. 1), an internal inconsistency we could not resolve. D is the number of annotated query–passage pairs (Sec. 3.1, 4.2).

**Paper says:** model-size law L(N) = (A/N)^α + δ (Eq. 6) with, for MS MARCO, A = 3.22e4, α = 0.53, δ = 0.04, R² = 0.991 (Table 1, Fig. 3). Data-size law L(D) = (B/D)^β + δ (Eq. 7) with B = 3.49e3, β = 1.05, δ = 0.05, R² = 0.954 (Table 2, Fig. 4), fitted on BERT-Base with up to all annotations. A joint law (Eq. 8) has A ≈ 3.6e4, B ≈ 7.1e3, α ≈ 0.56, β ≈ 1.31, δ ≈ 0.03 (Sec. 4.4, Eq. 9–10, Fig. 6). The constant δ is read as an irreducible loss (Sec. 4.1).

**Paper says:** the scaling holds for human labels and for three kinds of generated labels (ICT, docT5query, ChatGLM3); ICT has the smallest slope, and the Fig. 5 caption says ChatGLM3 has the steepest slope and passes human labels at 500K while the text says human labels give the best models (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 5). With the fitted joint law and a cost model, a $20,000 budget favours a model of about 13 billion parameters if inference cost is ignored, and million-scale models if it is included (Sec. 5, Fig. 7–8).

**Paper says (limitations, Sec. 6):** in-domain evaluation only, no hard negatives or distillation, single-vector retrievers only. The arXiv listing notes that v2 "fixes a bug in the experiments".

## 4. Our experiment

**Goal.** An inexpensive illustration of the two basic trends (loss vs N, loss vs D) with an honest error estimate. It is **not** a reproduction.

| Aspect | Paper (section / figure) | Our experiment |
|---|---|---|
| Task / data | MS MARCO passage (8.8M passages, 0.5M train queries) and T2Ranking (Sec. 3.3) | MS MARCO only; passage file truncated to 8,326,970 passages (94.18%) |
| Models | 24 Google BERT checkpoints 0.5M–82M non-emb. params; ERNIE for T2Ranking (Sec. 3.2) | 5 BERT checkpoints: Tiny, Mini, Small, Medium, Base (same family as the paper's red stars, Fig. 3) |
| N definition | non-embedding parameters (Sec. 3.2, footnote 2) | non-embedding incl. projection layer and unused BERT pooler (= the paper's Fig. 6 legend sizes when divided by 2^20) |
| D definition | number of annotated query–passage pairs (Sec. 3.1, 4.2) | number of (qid, pid) training pairs |
| Architecture | shared encoder + projection to 768; CLS or mean pooling (Sec. 3.2, Eq. 2) | shared BERT + mean pooling + Linear(H→768); no normalisation |
| Training loss | softmax cross-entropy, random + in-batch negatives (Sec. 3.4, Eq. 3) | same: 1 positive + 256 random negatives shared by the batch; mean CE; no temperature |
| Optimisation length | fixed 10,000 steps (Sec. 3.4) | 3 epochs → 60–939 steps (depends on D); 237 steps for the model sweep |
| lr / batch / optimiser | not stated in the paper (UNVERIFIED) | lr 1e-4, batch 128, AdamW, linear decay, warmup 10 steps, bf16 |
| Metric | contrastive entropy = −log softmax of the positive among 1+256 candidates (Sec. 3.5, Eq. 5) | same quantity (mean NLL, nats), K = 257 |
| Evaluation set | dev queries (~7,000, Sec. 3.3); 100,000-passage sub-corpus used for the metric study (Sec. 3.5) | first 1,000 dev.small queries by qid (1,086 pairs); 100,000-passage pool; 5 repeats; fixed eval seed 1 |
| Checkpoint reported | best test loss during training, no early stopping (Sec. 4.1) | final checkpoint after epoch 3 |
| Model sweep | full training set, many models (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 3) | D = 10,000 pairs, 5 models |
| Data sweep | BERT-Base, up to all ~500K annotations (Sec. 4.2, Fig. 4) | BERT-Small, D = 2,500 … 40,000 |
| Fit form | L = (A/N)^α + δ (Eq. 6); L = (B/D)^β + δ (Eq. 7); joint Eq. 8 | 3-param a·X^-α + c (same family; a = A^α) and a 2-param a·X^-α (extra, main) |
| Seeds | not stated (UNVERIFIED) | 3 training seeds 42/43/44; evaluation seed fixed |
| Annotation quality, budget allocation | Sec. 4.3 (ICT, docT5query, ChatGLM3), Sec. 5 | not reproduced |

**Data.** MS MARCO passage ranking. The corpus file has 8,326,970 passages (94.18% of the full collection; the file is cut at the end, ids 0…8,326,969). Of 532,751 unique training pairs, 3,311 (0.62%) point to missing passages and are dropped, leaving 529,440 pairs over 499,872 queries. D pairs are the first D of a seeded shuffle.

**Models.** Five Google BERT miniatures, parameters in Table A1 of the appendix; one shared encoder, mean pooling, Linear(H→768), dot-product score, no normalisation, no temperature (Figure F2).

**Training.** 3 epochs, lr 1e-4, batch 128, AdamW (weight decay 0.001, β2 0.999), linear decay, 10 warm-up steps, gradient clipping 1.0, bf16, gradient checkpointing. Per step, 256 random corpus passages are shared by the batch as negatives (K = 257). Settings are identical for all 27 runs (read from each run's `training_args.bin`).

**Evaluation.** The 1,000 dev.small queries with the smallest qids (1,086 query–positive pairs); a fixed pool of 100,000 passages drawn from the 8,325,884 passages that are not positives of those queries; for each pair, 256 negatives drawn from the pool, 5 repeats (5,430 draws per model); evaluation seed 1 for every model; the mean over pairs is the reported loss.

**Seeds.** Training seeds 42, 43, 44 change the projection initialisation, the data subset and order and the training negatives; the evaluation seed does not change.

**Hardware and time.** One NVIDIA RTX 5880 Ada Generation (49,140 MiB; driver 580.178.04, nvidia-smi on 2026-10-29); Intel Core Ultra 9 285K (24 logical CPUs), 93 GiB RAM; PyTorch 2.11.0+cu128, Transformers 4.52.4; peak GPU memory (allocated) 4645.6 MiB. Summed over the 27 runs: training 1966 s, evaluation 1368 s, total 3495 s (58.2 min). The last orchestrator session (seeds 43/44 and new configurations) lasted 51.1 min.

## 5. Audit results

### 5.1 Compliance summary

Verdicts and counts are in the box of Section 0; the complete matrix with evidence is `AUDIT_COMPLIANCE_MATRIX.md`. Group C is the one that limits what may be claimed.

### 5.2 Findings about the code

**Code does:** the architecture in `modeling.py` is unchanged from the original repository (the file is byte-identical). Mean pooling, Linear(H→768), plain dot product, no temperature, cross-entropy over 1 positive and 256 shared random negatives, mean over the batch (`modeling.py` lines 47–72, 112–118).

**Code does:** `contrastive_perplexity` computes, per (query, positive) pair, the cross-entropy over 1 + 256 candidates and averages the pair losses and the 5 repeats. There is no `exp`, so the value is an NLL in nats, not a perplexity. Chance level is ln(257) = 5.549; our worst model has 0.131 of this and our best 0.028. For reference only, exp of the mean is 2.068 for the worst model and 1.171 for the best.

**Code does:** training and evaluation both use K = 257 and the same formula, but the training loss in the logs is a running mean over the whole run, computed in train mode (dropout) with bf16 on pairs already seen. The final dev loss is computed on the final model in eval mode with fp32 on held-out queries. They are **not comparable**; the training curves (F8) show the training loss still falling at the end, and the last-window training loss for BERT-Small (0.0555) is far below its dev loss (0.2345), but this cannot be called over-fitting without a like-for-like measurement (for example evaluating the final model in eval mode on held-out training queries, not done here).

**Code does:** changes from the original repository are limited to paths, robust file reading, a missing-argument fix, checkpoint saving, optional pre-loaded data, a 1,000-query evaluation cap and a multi-seed orchestrator (see `CHANGES.md`). None of them alters the loss, the model or the metric definition; the cap on queries and the pool size are intentional scale-downs.

**Our audit shows:** no query leaks from training into evaluation (train qids ∩ dev qids = 0, ∩ the evaluation qids = 0, identical query texts = 0). D subsets are nested within a seed and independent across seeds (10,000-pair overlaps 203–207 against 189 expected by chance). The evaluation pool is identical for every model (rebuild check, sha1 prefix f965e175b62f). The 1,000-query evaluation subset is a bit unrepresentative: mean query length 5.30 words versus 6.03 for the other dev queries.

**Our audit shows:** the missing 5.8% of the corpus are the highest passage ids. Lost training pairs belong to slightly shorter queries (5.74 vs 5.97 words); dev loses nothing. Impact is judged low, though whether ids carry any topical order is UNVERIFIED. The training pair file has 10 duplicated lines (532,761 lines, 532,751 unique pairs).

**Our audit shows:** the non-embedding count used for N includes the unused BERT pooler and the projection layer. In units of 2^20 the five sizes are 0.5, 3.3, 12.7, 24.7, 82.2 M, exactly the labels in the paper's Fig. 6 legend, so the counting convention agrees with the paper. Our x-axes use 10^6 units.

### 5.3 Independent recomputation (from the 27 JSON files)

Means and standard deviations (SD, ddof = 1) come from the JSON files, which agree with `results.csv` (max difference 0.0e+00) and `results_summary.csv` (rounding only). There are 9 distinct configurations (not 10: BERT-Small with D = 10,000 belongs to both sweeps). Fits: all six SUMMARY values reproduce to the printed precision.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model size N | 2-param  L = a·X^-α (OLS in log–log) | 34.79 | 0.299 | — | 0.9858 | 0.9867 | main fit |
| Model size N | 3-param  L = a·X^-α + c (curve_fit) | 206.29 | 0.440 | 0.093 | — | 0.9991 | bound flags: none; 5 points, 3 parameters |

| Data size D | 3-param  L = a·X^-α + c (curve_fit) | 8.97 | 0.444 | 0.084 | — | 0.9918 | bound flags: none; 5 points, 3 parameters |

The 3-parameter fits reach the same optimum from all 27 starting points (model) and 27 (data), with or without bounds, and touch no bound. **However** they have 2 degrees of freedom: leave-one-out gives 3-parameter exponents of 0.426–0.492 (model) and 0.260–0.770 (data, with 1 fit hitting the bound c ≥ 0); per-seed fits give 0.367–0.489 and 0.247–0.669. The 2-parameter exponents are much steadier: leave-one-out 0.259–0.320 and 0.267–0.294, per seed 0.292–0.307 and 0.258–0.310 (Figure F9, Tables A2–A3). Counting parameters without the output layer gives a model exponent of 0.288 instead of 0.299.

Why it is not a like-for-like comparison: (i) 237 steps against 10,000 (Sec. 3.4); (ii) D from 2,500 to 40,000 on BERT-Small against up to about 500K on BERT-Base (Sec. 4.2, Fig. 4); (iii) final checkpoint against best test loss (Sec. 4.1); (iv) smaller evaluation set; (v) fits on 5 points with 3 free parameters. The exponents are lower than the paper's, and both our constants (0.093, 0.084) are larger than the paper's (0.04, 0.05). We draw no conclusion from these differences.

## 7. Discussion

**Same direction as the paper?** Within this small scope, yes in direction: loss decreases as N and D increase (paper: Fig. 3, Fig. 4). Nothing stronger may be said: the exponents, constants and fit qualities are not comparable with Tables 1–2 (Section 5.3), and nothing here tests annotation quality (Sec. 4.3) or budget allocation (Sec. 5).

**Differences from the paper.** Short schedules (237 steps for the model sweep), final-not-best checkpoint, smaller evaluation, BERT-Small for the data sweep, one dataset. In such short runs larger models learn faster per step (F8), so the model-size curve mixes capacity and speed of learning; the data sweep mixes data and steps.

**Limitations.** Five points per sweep, three seeds; a 3-parameter fit with 2 degrees of freedom; no test of extrapolation; no hard negatives; corpus truncated; the evaluation set is the 1,000 smallest qids; the learning rate was chosen from two values with an almost untrained model (losses 5.4256 and 4.9708 against chance 5.549).

**Threats to validity.** *Internal:* training length differs across D; evaluation seed fixed (SD excludes evaluation sampling); early seed-42 runs were produced before the orchestrator was rewritten (their configuration was verified from `training_args.bin`). *External:* one dataset, one model family, in-domain only. *Construct:* contrastive entropy with 256 random negatives measures random-negative discrimination, not ranking quality (the paper also notes the metrics are not equivalent, Sec. 6).

## 8. How to reproduce

```
# training + evaluation (original orchestrator, background run)
export MSMARCO_DIR=<path to MS MARCO files>
cd drscale_exp && nohup python3 run_all.py > logs/run.log 2>&1 &
# audit and package (from deliverables/scripts)
python3 -I audit_data.py; python3 -I audit_model.py; python3 -I audit_config.py
python3 -I recompute.py; python3 -I make_figures.py; python3 -I build_docs.py; python3 -I check_numbers.py
```

Environment: Python 3.11.7, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu128, Transformers 4.52.4, NumPy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.16.3, pandas 2.3.3, Matplotlib 3.10.6; original repository `jingtaozhan/DRScale`, commit `81453c3b67486641ad282d58f819392a08561e77`. Training is not bit-for-bit deterministic on GPU, so re-running will give slightly different losses.

**A4. Glossary.** *NLL / contrastive entropy*: negative log of the softmax probability of the positive. *Nat*: unit of NLL with natural log. *Non-embedding parameters*: parameters excluding word/position embeddings. *SD*: sample standard deviation with n − 1. *R²*: fraction of variance explained by the fit. *Seed*: number that fixes a random generator. *bf16*: 16-bit floating-point format used during training.

**A5. Raw data.** `data/results/*.json` (one file per run), `data/results.csv`, `data/results_summary.csv`, `data/figure_data/*.csv`, `data/run.log`, `data/status.json`, `tables/`, `audit/`.
